opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, at the time I didn't overthink it as much as people might expect. When I was applying for PhD programs, of course I looked at rankings, and UCSD was not at the very top tier the way Stanford, Berkeley, or CMU were. And yes, there was some talk that a few faculty in the vision area had left or were thinking of leaving, so people around me would ask, "Are you sure this is a good choice?"

But I think what mattered most to me was the advisor, not the school's name. When I talked with Zhuowen Tu, I felt there was a real fit. He was very open, very curious, and he gave students a lot of freedom to explore their own ideas. For a PhD, you spend five or six years working closely with one person, so that relationship is much more important than whether the department is ranked third or fifteenth.

I also had a feeling, maybe a bit naive, that a slightly smaller group could actually be an advantage. In a huge, famous lab, you can easily become one small part of a big machine. In a smaller environment, you have more chances to own a project, make mistakes, and figure things out yourself. That kind of independence turned out to be really valuable for me later.

And looking back, the field was changing so fast, deep learning was just starting to take off, that the traditional rankings didn't really capture where the interesting work would happen. What mattered was whether you could find good problems and have the space to work on them. So my advice to students now is similar: rankings and faculty movement are real signals, you shouldn't ignore them, but they shouldn't override the question of whether you'll grow with the person you're working with.

r001.rationale: He says the advisor relationship mattered much more than the department’s rank and describes his fit with Zhuowen Tu.

r002.rationale: He emphasizes having space to explore his own ideas and find good problems to work on, saying rankings did not capture where interesting work would happen.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I didn't think about rankings much at all. When I was choosing a PhD program, what mattered to me was the advisor and the environment, not where the school sat on some list. I went to UCSD to work with Zhuowen Tu, and that decision was really about him and about the research direction, which was computer vision and the early stages of what became deep learning.

The faculty departures were real, I'm not going to pretend they weren't. Around that time a lot of strong vision and machine learning people were being pulled toward industry or toward other schools. But I think I was a bit naive, in a good way. I was a student from Shanghai Jiao Tong who just wanted a chance to do research in the US, and UCSD gave me that. I wasn't calculating the long-term prestige value. I was thinking, can I learn here, will my advisor have time for me, is there a group of people doing interesting work.

Looking back, I actually think being in a smaller or less "hot" place had advantages. There was less noise. You weren't competing with twenty other students for the same problem. And San Diego is close to the Bay Area and to LA, so collaborations and internships were easy to reach. A lot of what shaped my career came from internships at places like Facebook AI Research and Adobe, and those happened because my advisor encouraged me to go out and because I had the space to explore.

So my honest answer is that ranking and departures were things other people worried about on my behalf. For me the question was simpler: is there someone here who will push me to do good work? There was, and that was enough.

r001.rationale: He says the advisor and research environment mattered more than rankings and that he chose UCSD to work with Zhuowen Tu.

r002.rationale: He emphasizes pursuing computer vision research, learning, and working on interesting problems as his priorities over the school’s ranking.

astra-6.text:
I think those were reasonable concerns, but I didn’t want to make the decision based on ranking alone. A ranking gives you a broad impression of a university; it doesn’t necessarily tell you what your experience as a PhD student will be. That depends much more on whom you work with, what problems you can pursue, and whether the environment helps you grow.

The faculty departures mattered in that same concrete sense: would there still be people I could learn from and do research with? I wouldn’t simply dismiss that concern, but I also wouldn’t treat a departure as a verdict on the whole department. For me, the key was whether UCSD offered the right research fit. You can’t eliminate all the uncertainty—you have to decide which factors matter most to you.

r001.rationale: The response says the PhD experience depends “much more” on whom he works with than on ranking alone, presenting collaborator choice as more important.

r002.rationale: The response says the experience depends “much more” on which problems he can pursue than on ranking alone, presenting desired research work as more important.

sol-6.1.text:
At the time, I definitely had concerns. When you’re applying from China, rankings are one of the easiest things to look at, and hearing that faculty were leaving adds uncertainty. But ultimately, you’re choosing a place to do research, so the more important question is who you’ll work with and whether that environment fits you.

For me, the opportunity to work with Zhuowen Tu mattered much more than the overall ranking. I was interested in his research, and I felt I could learn a lot from him. Faculty departures were something to consider, but they didn’t erase that opportunity. I couldn’t predict exactly how everything would turn out; I just felt that the research fit was a stronger reason to go than the ranking was a reason not to.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly says working with Zhuowen Tu mattered much more than UCSD’s overall ranking.

r002.rationale: It says Xie was interested in Tu’s research and that research fit was a stronger reason to go than the ranking was a reason not to.
